newsitem.title: MALI: Mali - cradle of a Middle Ages empire built on gold.
newsitem.headline: Mali - cradle of a Middle Ages empire built on gold.

text.p: Mali, first stop on U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher's first tour of Sub-Saharan Africa, was the cradle of an African empire which was built on gold and flourished while Europe was in the Middle Ages.
Today, the sprawling, mainly Moslem West African nation is one of the poorest on earth, struggling against drought and the implacable advance of the Sahara desert.
Malians heading for the bright lights of Europe are at the heart of former colonial power France's fight to halt illegal immigration from the world's poorest continent.

But after a successful transition from one-party rule to democracy in 1992, an economic liberalisation programme that has won plaudits from the World Bank and lively foreign interest in its gold, the future is starting to look more promising.
Word of the wealth of the mighty 13th and 14th century empire of Mali, from which the modern Mali took its name on independence in 1960, captured the imagination of the rich and powerful in Europe.
When Mansa (ruler) Moussa made a pilgrimage to Mecca in the 14th century, he took eight tonnes of gold which he liberally dispensed in Cairo causing the price of the metal to collapse.
Some historians say it was talk of the wealth of the Malian city of Djenne which brought the first European explorers -- the Portuguese -- and their ships to the coast of West Africa.
France began to conquer what is now modern day Mali in the late 19th century.
Independence leader Modibo Keita steered the country on a pro-Soviet course until his removal in 1968 by army officers led by Moussa Traore, who went on to rule over a one-party state.
Mali embraced multi-party democracy after the army ousted Traore in 1991 following violent pro-democracy demonstrations in which more than 200 people were killed.

A transitional military government led by Lieutenant-Colonel Amadou Toumani Toure stepped down after elections won by historian Alpha Oumar Konare and his Alliance for Democracy in Mali (ADEMA) party.

Light-skinned Tuareg nomads -- who controlled the Middle Ages caravan routes across the Sahara -- rebelled against the black-dominated government in 1990 but the two sides sealed peace last March with a huge bonfire of weapons in the ancient city of Timbuktu.
On the economic front, the World Bank predicts that Mali will be Africa's third largest gold exporter by 1998.

But its 9.4 million people remain poor with a per capita annual income of just $250. The average life expectancy is 46, just 17 percent of adults can read and write and and only 37 percent have access to safe water, according to U.N. estimates.
Konare faces fresh parliamentary and presidential elections in the first half of 1997.
